findings.title: MCP rate limiter keyed per-token/per-client, not per-user — a user multiplies their budget by minting extra MCP tokens
findings.description: The MCP per-minute limiter keys the counter on `format!("{}:{}", principal.client_id, principal.user_id)` (server/src/mcp/routes.rs:825), then admits against that key in mcp/rate_limit.rs:admit_request. For personal MCP tokens the middleware sets `client_id = format!("mcp_token:{}", token_row.id)` (server/src/middleware/mcp_auth.rs:136), so every distinct personal token produces a distinct rate-limit bucket even though they all belong to the same user. Personal MCP tokens are self-service (db/mcp_tokens.rs:create_mcp_token, routes/mcp_tokens.rs) with no visible per-user cap. The same is true for OAuth clients when dynamic client registration is enabled (oauth/routes.rs:274 register_client mints a fresh `swole_...` client_id).
findings.attackOrTrigger: An authenticated user creates N personal MCP tokens from /settings (or, with allow_dynamic_client_registration, registers N OAuth clients and authorizes each). Each token/client yields a different `client_id`, hence a separate bucket. Their effective request ceiling becomes N x MCP_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE (default 60) instead of a single per-user 60/min, defeating the throttle whose purpose is to cap a single account's/agent's request volume against the DB.
findings.why: The limiter is intended to bound how hard one authenticated principal (an AI agent) can hammer the backend. Keying on the token/client id rather than user_id makes the cap trivially multipliable by the same actor, so the DoS protection it provides per account is only as strong as one token's worth.
findings.fixSketch: Key the MCP limiter on `principal.user_id` alone (or add a second per-user bucket alongside the per-token one) so all of a user's tokens share one budget, and/or cap the number of active MCP tokens per user.

findings.title: request_ip trusts X-Real-IP unconditionally — direct exposure allows login rate-limit bypass and unbounded map growth
findings.description: request_ip (server/src/auth/rate_limit.rs:26-45) prefers the client-supplied `X-Real-IP` header over the real peer socket with no trusted-proxy gate (no TRUSTED_PROXY flag, no peer-CIDR check). This value is the sole key for the login/OAuth per-IP failure limiter (routes/auth.rs:34-79, oauth/routes.rs:409-513). The bundled nginx overwrites the header with `$remote_addr` (client/nginx.conf:29/38/47/56), so behind that proxy it is safe. But the server binds 0.0.0.0 (server/src/main.rs:545); if the port is ever published directly (or a proxy that does not overwrite the header is used), the header becomes attacker-controlled.
findings.attackOrTrigger: With the port reachable without the bundled nginx, an attacker sends each brute-force login with a fresh forged `X-Real-IP` (e.g. random values). Because is_ip_rate_limited/record_ip_failure key on that value, every request is a brand-new IP: the per-IP failure counter never accumulates, so the limiter is fully bypassed for password spraying and username enumeration (the unknown-user path at routes/auth.rs:45-52 has no per-user lockout to fall back on). Simultaneously, each distinct forged IP inserts a new HashMap entry in LOGIN_FAILURES_BY_IP; evict_stale only drops entries older than the window (default 10 min), so an attacker can hold unbounded distinct keys in memory within a window -> memory-exhaustion DoS.
findings.why: The per-IP limiter is the only brute-force defense for non-existent usernames and for password spraying across many accounts (per-user lockout does not help those). Trusting a forgeable header removes that defense and adds an unbounded-map DoS the moment the deployment topology differs from the assumed nginx setup. Prior audit SEC-3 flagged the same trust as theoretical-but-real.
findings.fixSketch: Gate X-Real-IP trust behind an explicit TRUSTED_PROXY env flag (or verify req.peer_addr() is within a configured trusted-proxy CIDR before honoring the header); otherwise fall back to peer_addr(). This closes both the bypass and the memory growth.

findings.title: Login limiter check-then-record is non-atomic (two separate lock acquisitions), unlike the MCP limiter
findings.description: The login/OAuth flow reads the counter with is_ip_rate_limited (its own Mutex lock, rate_limit.rs:59) at routes/auth.rs:37 / oauth/routes.rs:454, and only later records a failure via record_ip_failure (a second, separate lock, rate_limit.rs:74) at routes/auth.rs:47/71 and oauth/routes.rs:466/503. There is no single critical section spanning check-and-record. By contrast the MCP limiter's admit_request (mcp/rate_limit.rs:20-39) does check-and-push atomically under one lock.
findings.attackOrTrigger: Multiple concurrent login attempts from the same IP each acquire the read lock, all observe a count below max_attempts before any of them has recorded its failure, and all proceed. Under concurrency the effective number of admitted failing attempts can exceed the configured LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT_ATTEMPTS by roughly the in-flight concurrency, loosening the limit.
findings.why: It is a genuine time-of-check/time-of-use gap that lets the configured limit be overshot; impact is bounded because each attempt still performs an expensive argon2 verify (self-throttling on CPU) and per-user DB lockout provides a second layer, so it is only a minor hardening/correctness gap rather than a clean bypass.
findings.fixSketch: Fold the check and the increment into a single admit-style function that takes one lock and both counts and records (mirroring MCP admit_request), returning whether the attempt is admitted.
